screens.title: Spawning Objects and Object Pooling
screens.narratorSegment: In real games you often create and remove many similar objects: bullets, enemies, particles, or pickups. Those operations are simple to code with Unity's Instantiate and Destroy, but they allocate and free memory repeatedly. That leads to garbage-collection spikes that cause frame drops, especially on mobile hardware. In this lesson you'll learn the concrete mechanics of Instantiate and Destroy, why Destroy is not immediate, and how object pooling replaces allocation with reuse to avoid GC spikes. We'll walk through a basic object pool implementation, how to get and return pooled objects safely, and how pooled objects reset state when reactivated. You'll also see common mistakes to avoid, like forgetting to reset velocity or leaving objects active when returning them. By the end you'll be able to choose when pooling matters, implement a simple pool for bullets, and test it under heavy load to confirm smoother performance. Think of pooling as keeping a ready bucket of objects you reuse, rather than throwing away and remaking them each frame.

screens.title: Instantiate(): creating runtime instances
screens.narratorSegment: Instantiate is Unity's runtime factory: given a Prefab template it creates a new GameObject instance with all components, child objects, and initial property values configured in the Prefab asset. When you call Instantiate you can specify a position, rotation, and optionally a parent transform to organize the instance in the Hierarchy. For example, when firing a weapon you commonly call Instantiate with a bullet Prefab and a fire point transform to spawn a projectile. Behind the scenes Instantiate allocates memory for the new GameObject and its components, runs initialization code, and adds the instance to the scene. That allocation is inexpensive when done occasionally, but when many objects are created per second the repeated memory allocation contributes to garbage and eventual GC activity. A common misconception is that Instantiate is free because it is a single line of code. In practice it triggers allocation and initialization work. Concrete example: calling Instantiate(bulletPrefab, firePoint. position, firePoint. rotation); spawns a separate bullet instance each time, which must later be cleaned up by Destroy or reused by a pool. Takeaway question: when will creating new instances frequently become a measurable cost in your game?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Instantiate Explained
What Instantiate does
  • Clones a Prefab with components and children.
  • Allocates fresh memory for the instance and its components.
  • Registers the new object in the Scene Hierarchy.
  • Accepts position, rotation, and optional parent.
Concrete Example
Instantiate(bulletPrefab, firePoint.position, firePoint.rotation); spawns a new bullet using the Prefab as a template.
Common Misconception

Instantiate is not free; its allocations accumulate when called many times per second.

Code Example
// Spawn a bullet at the fire point
Instantiate(bulletPrefab, firePoint.position, firePoint.rotation);
Why it matters

Repeated Instantiate calls allocate memory and increase garbage. When many instances are created per second, you should consider pooling to avoid runtime stalls.

screens.title: Destroy(): marking objects for removal
screens.narratorSegment: Destroy removes a GameObject from the scene, optionally after a delay. When you call Destroy(gameObject) the object is marked for destruction; Unity performs the actual cleanup at the end of the frame or during the engine's internal cleanup cycle. This delayed behavior is important: attempting to access components or properties of a GameObject after you call Destroy can lead to invalid references or unexpected behavior because the object may already be considered dead by the engine. Destroy(gameObject, 3f) schedules the removal after three seconds, which is useful for self-cleanup but still results in eventual deallocation. A misconception is thinking Destroy immediately frees memory and removes every trace; in fact it only flags the object for removal and the memory will be reclaimed by the runtime, which may trigger garbage-collection work later. For high-frequency objects, relying on Destroy repeatedly compounds allocation and deallocation work, increasing GC pressure. Instead, pooled objects should call SetActive(false) to disable behavior and avoid allocation. Practical takeaway: use Destroy for occasional, single-use objects, but prefer pooling for repeated fast spawns. Destroy(): marking objects for removal means destroy schedules removal and eventual deallocation; it is not instantaneous and contributes to gc when used frequently.. In practical terms, how destroy schedules cleanup and why you must avoid immediate access afterward. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Destroy Explained
What Destroy does
  • Flags a GameObject for removal from the scene.
  • Actual cleanup happens at end of frame or during GC cycles.
  • Accepts an optional delay before the flag is set.
  • Accessing a destroyed object in the same frame can be unsafe.
Safety Note

Do not assume Destroy frees memory instantly. Replace Destroy in pooled objects with a return-to-pool pattern to avoid deallocation altogether.

Example
// Remove after 3 seconds
Destroy(gameObject, 3f);
Misconception check

Destroying many objects per second still causes memory churn because destruction participates in runtime cleanup. For repeated items, prefer pooling to avoid that churn.

screens.title: Why frequent Instantiate/Destroy hurts performance
screens.narratorSegment: Repeatedly creating and destroying objects generates many short-lived allocations. Each Instantiate creates memory for the GameObject and its components. Each Destroy eventually frees that memory. The garbage collector monitors memory usage and periodically reclaims unreferenced memory; when many objects are allocated and deallocated in a short period the GC triggers a larger and more frequent collection. These GC spikes pause execution briefly while the runtime reclaims memory, producing visible stutters or frame drops. The problem is most acute on platforms with constrained memory and slower collectors, like mobile devices. A concrete example: a bullet-hell shooter that Instantiates hundreds of projectiles per second will show many allocations and brief frame pauses as GC runs. A common misconception is that small objects do not matter. In aggregate they do. The practical response is to reduce allocations by reusing objects via pooling. Another strategy is to avoid generating temporary garbage in frequently called code paths. Takeaway: measure allocations, then convert high-frequency spawn/despawn objects to a pool to smooth runtime performance. content.html:
Performance › Allocation & GC › Why it hurts
Step-by-step impact
  1. Instantiate allocates memory for the object graph.
  2. Destroy marks the object for cleanup; memory becomes collectible.
  3. Garbage collector runs and pauses execution to reclaim memory.
  4. Repeated cycles cause frequent pauses and visible frame drops.
Concrete Example

A shooter that Instantiates many bullets per second will allocate quickly and force GC runs, creating stutter unless bullets are reused.

Mitigations
  • Use object pooling to reuse instances instead of reallocating.
  • Avoid temporary allocations in hot update loops.
  • Measure with the Profiler to find allocation hotspots.
Key Takeaway

Reducing allocations lowers GC frequency and results in smoother frames.

screens.title: Object Pool architecture and components
screens.narratorSegment: A basic object pool holds a collection of pre-instantiated GameObjects and exposes methods to get and return them. The common components are a prefab reference, an initial pool size, a list or queue to store pooled instances, and two public methods: GetPooledObject and ReturnPooledObject. In Awake you instantiate the initial set of objects, call SetActive(false) on each, and add them to the list. GetPooledObject searches the list for an inactive object, activates and returns it, and optionally expands the pool if none are available. ReturnPooledObject deactivates the object via SetActive(false) and optionally resets state. Pools often use a singleton pattern for easy access, but be cautious with singletons in larger architectures. Communication with pooled objects happens via lifecycle callbacks: OnEnable is used to reset state when an object is activated, and OnDisable cancels timers or scheduled returns. Concrete example: ObjectPool. Instance. GetPooledObject returns a bullet which the player positions and activates; when the bullet collides it calls ObjectPool. Instance. ReturnPooledObject instead of Destroy. Misconception: pools eliminate the need to manage state — in reality you must explicitly reset any mutable fields. How will you ensure every pooled object begins clean?

keyIdea.text: A pool contains a prefab, an initial set of inactive instances, and Get/Return methods; OnEnable/OnDisable reset state when reusing objects.

content.html:
Pool › Architecture › Components
Core Components
  • Prefab reference (the template to clone for initial pool).
  • poolSize: number to instantiate in Awake.
  • List<GameObject> or Queue<GameObject> to hold instances.
  • GetPooledObject and ReturnPooledObject public methods.
Singleton Pattern
Often used so other scripts call ObjectPool.Instance.GetPooledObject() directly, but keep singletons simple and well-documented.
Lifecycle Integration
Awake: instantiate pool and SetActive(false).
GetPooledObject: find inactive, SetActive(true), return and let OnEnable reset state.
ReturnPooledObject: SetActive(false) and optionally reset or reposition.
Concrete Flow

PlayerAttack requests a projectile, sets its position and rotation, and the projectile's OnEnable sets velocity and lifetime. On collision the projectile calls ReturnToPool.

screens.title: ObjectPool.cs — a basic implementation
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concise ObjectPool implementation. The pool holds a public prefab reference and poolSize configured in the Inspector. Awake uses a loop to Instantiate the initial objects, call SetActive(false), and add them to the pooledObjects list. GetPooledObject iterates over pooledObjects, checks activeInHierarchy, activates and returns the first inactive object. If no inactive object is found the example optionally Instantiates a new object, adds it to the list, and logs a warning that the pool expanded. ReturnPooledObject simply SetActive(false) to deactivate and return the object to the pool; you may also reset state here. A common pitfall is missing SetActive(false) when returning an object, causing the pool to incorrectly consider objects active and leak resources. The snippet provided is intentionally straightforward: it demonstrates the flow and allows you to extend it with queues, circular indices, or thread-safe patterns. Concrete example: use this pool for bullets by calling ObjectPool. Instance. GetPooledObject in your attack method and setting position and rotation before the object is used. Think about how you would add a maximum pool cap or prewarm of child components.

keyIdea.title: Implementation Idea
keyIdea.text: A simple pool preinstantiates inactive objects, hands them out on request, and deactivates them on return. Expand or optimize as needed.

content.html:
Code › ObjectPool.cs
ObjectPool (excerpt)
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

public class ObjectPool : MonoBehaviour
{
    public static ObjectPool Instance;
    public GameObject objectPrefab;
    public int poolSize = 20;
    private List<GameObject> pooledObjects;

    void Awake()
    {
        if (Instance == null) Instance = this; else { Destroy(gameObject); return; }
        pooledObjects = new List<GameObject>();
        for (int i = 0; i < poolSize; i++)
        {
            GameObject obj = Instantiate(objectPrefab);
            obj.SetActive(false);
            pooledObjects.Add(obj);
        }
    }

    public GameObject GetPooledObject()
    {
        foreach (GameObject obj in pooledObjects)
        {
            if (!obj.activeInHierarchy)
            {
                obj.SetActive(true);
                return obj;
            }
        }
        Debug.LogWarning("Object pool exhausted. Instantiating new object: " + objectPrefab.name);
        GameObject newObj = Instantiate(objectPrefab);
        pooledObjects.Add(newObj);
        return newObj;
    }

    public void ReturnPooledObject(GameObject obj)
    {
        obj.SetActive(false);
    }
}
Walkthrough Notes
  • Singleton Instance for global access.
  • Prewarm pool in Awake and deactivate each object.
  • Search list for inactive objects on each Get request.
  • Warn and expand pool if exhausted.
Extension Ideas
Use queues or ring buffers for O(1) access, reset internal state when returning, or implement an upper cap to avoid unbounded growth.

The ProjectilePooled example shows how to use OnEnable to clear velocity, set damage, and apply a fresh force. OnEnable is called when a GameObject becomes active; this is the ideal place to reset timers, clear physics velocities, and schedule a ReturnToPool after a lifetime using Invoke. OnDisable should cancel invokes and clean up any references so the object remains safe while inactive. In collisions the projectile calls ReturnToPool instead of Destroy, ensuring it goes back to the pool and becomes available for reuse. A common mistake is to assume the constructor or Awake will reset state; Awake runs only once at load time, not each activation. Concrete example: in OnEnable set rb. velocity = Vector3. zero and then rb. AddForce(transform. forward * speed) to ensure the projectile always starts fresh. Misconception: pooling guarantees fresh behavior; in reality you must explicitly reset every variable that can carry over from previous uses. void OnEnable()
{
    if (rb != null)
    {
        rb.velocity = Vector3.zero;
        rb.angularVelocity = Vector3.zero;
        rb.AddForce(transform.forward * speed, ForceMode.VelocityChange);

    Invoke("ReturnToPool", lifetime);
}

void OnDisable()
{
    CancelInvoke("ReturnToPool");
}

{
    // Handle damage...
    ReturnToPool();
}

screens.title: Pooling vs Instantiate/Destroy
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a naive Instantiate/Destroy approach and an object pool depends on frequency and platform constraints. Instantiate/Destroy is simple to implement and fine for occasional spawns such as rare pickups or one-off effects. It keeps code minimal but causes allocation overhead when used frequently. Object pooling requires more upfront work: preinstantiation, reset logic, and management of active/inactive state. The benefit is lower runtime allocation and fewer GC spikes, which translates to smoother frame rates in high-frequency scenarios. There are tradeoffs: pools consume memory for the precreated objects and may need careful sizing or dynamic expansion to avoid exhaustion. A misconception is that pools always save memory; in fact you trade memory headroom for runtime stability. Concrete scenario: for debris from a single explosion that spawns hundreds of fragments, a pool prevents repeated allocation spikes; for a rare boss drop used once each level, Instantiate/Destroy is acceptable. Key decision factors are spawn rate, object complexity, and target hardware. Final question: what is the expected spawn rate in your scene and does that justify the memory cost of a pool? screens.title: Common pooling mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Object pooling fixes allocation costs but introduces its own class of bugs if not implemented carefully. The most frequent mistakes are failing to reset an object's state, forgetting to call SetActive(false) when returning an object, and leaving Destroy calls in pooled objects. Failing to reset state might leave a projectile with previous velocity or an enemy with reduced health. Forgetting to deactivate means the pool will think the object is still active and may appear duplicated or leak behavior. Leaving Destroy in pooled code undoes the benefit of pooling by causing deallocation. Another pitfall is not planning for pool exhaustion: if your pool lacks dynamic expansion you may run out of objects at runtime. The provided pool logs a warning and creates a new instance if none are available, which is helpful during testing. Also avoid putting heavy initialization in Awake that assumes fresh instances; prefer OnEnable for runtime resets. Concrete practice: audit each pooled script and list any fields that persist across uses, then explicitly reset them on enable. Takeaway: pooling helps performance but requires deliberate, testable reset and return logic.

fullNarratorScript:
In real games you often create and remove many similar objects: bullets, enemies, particles, or pickups. Those operations are simple to code with Unity's Instantiate and Destroy, but they allocate and free memory repeatedly. That leads to garbage-collection spikes that cause frame drops, especially on mobile hardware. In this lesson you'll learn the concrete mechanics of Instantiate and Destroy, why Destroy is not immediate, and how object pooling replaces allocation with reuse to avoid GC spikes. We'll walk through a basic object pool implementation, how to get and return pooled objects safely, and how pooled objects reset state when reactivated. You'll also see common mistakes to avoid, like forgetting to reset velocity or leaving objects active when returning them. By the end you'll be able to choose when pooling matters, implement a simple pool for bullets, and test it under heavy load to confirm smoother performance. Think of pooling as keeping a ready bucket of objects you reuse, rather than throwing away and remaking them each frame.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to create and manage GameObjects at runtime, recognize when naive creation becomes a performance problem, and implement a basic object pool to avoid frequent allocation. First, you'll learn to use Instantiate to spawn Prefab instances and Destroy to remove them safely. Then you'll learn to observe that Destroy does not immediately free memory, which leads to garbage-collection spikes when many objects are created and destroyed quickly. Next you'll implement an ObjectPool that preinstantiates a set of inactive objects, retrieves and returns them via GetPooledObject and ReturnPooledObject, and resets state on OnEnable to ensure predictable behavior. Finally, you'll learn to choose pool sizes, allow optional dynamic expansion, and test under heavy load. Each objective includes a small practice milestone so you can verify competency: spawning bullets, replacing Instantiate calls with pooled retrieval, and confirming smoother runtime when under sustained fire.

This second objectives slide drills into implementation and verification. You will implement an ObjectPool script, preinstantiate a configurable pool size in Awake, and expose GetPooledObject and ReturnPooledObject methods for use by your attack code. You will wire your PlayerAttack to request pooled projectiles rather than calling Instantiate. You will adapt the Projectile script to call ReturnToPool instead of Destroy, and use OnEnable to reset velocity and schedule a return after a lifetime. Testing is critical: run continuous fire and watch the Hierarchy to confirm that objects are activated and deactivated instead of being created and destroyed. Observe the Debug. LogWarning message when the pool is exhausted if you enable dynamic expansion. Finally, you will learn how to size a pool, when to allow dynamic growth, and how to avoid mistakes such as leaving objects active when returned. Each step is a small testable milestone so you can measure improvement.

Instantiate is Unity's runtime factory: given a Prefab template it creates a new GameObject instance with all components, child objects, and initial property values configured in the Prefab asset. When you call Instantiate you can specify a position, rotation, and optionally a parent transform to organize the instance in the Hierarchy. For example, when firing a weapon you commonly call Instantiate with a bullet Prefab and a fire point transform to spawn a projectile. Behind the scenes Instantiate allocates memory for the new GameObject and its components, runs initialization code, and adds the instance to the scene. That allocation is inexpensive when done occasionally, but when many objects are created per second the repeated memory allocation contributes to garbage and eventual GC activity. A common misconception is that Instantiate is free because it is a single line of code. In practice it triggers allocation and initialization work. Concrete example: calling Instantiate(bulletPrefab, firePoint. position, firePoint. rotation); spawns a separate bullet instance each time, which must later be cleaned up by Destroy or reused by a pool. Takeaway question: when will creating new instances frequently become a measurable cost in your game?

Destroy removes a GameObject from the scene, optionally after a delay. When you call Destroy(gameObject) the object is marked for destruction; Unity performs the actual cleanup at the end of the frame or during the engine's internal cleanup cycle. This delayed behavior is important: attempting to access components or properties of a GameObject after you call Destroy can lead to invalid references or unexpected behavior because the object may already be considered dead by the engine. Destroy(gameObject, 3f) schedules the removal after three seconds, which is useful for self-cleanup but still results in eventual deallocation. A misconception is thinking Destroy immediately frees memory and removes every trace; in fact it only flags the object for removal and the memory will be reclaimed by the runtime, which may trigger garbage-collection work later. For high-frequency objects, relying on Destroy repeatedly compounds allocation and deallocation work, increasing GC pressure. Instead, pooled objects should call SetActive(false) to disable behavior and avoid allocation. Practical takeaway: use Destroy for occasional, single-use objects, but prefer pooling for repeated fast spawns. Destroy(): marking objects for removal means destroy schedules removal and eventual deallocation; it is not instantaneous and contributes to gc when used frequently.. In practical terms, how destroy schedules cleanup and why you must avoid immediate access afterward. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Repeatedly creating and destroying objects generates many short-lived allocations. Each Instantiate creates memory for the GameObject and its components. Each Destroy eventually frees that memory. The garbage collector monitors memory usage and periodically reclaims unreferenced memory; when many objects are allocated and deallocated in a short period the GC triggers a larger and more frequent collection. These GC spikes pause execution briefly while the runtime reclaims memory, producing visible stutters or frame drops. The problem is most acute on platforms with constrained memory and slower collectors, like mobile devices. A concrete example: a bullet-hell shooter that Instantiates hundreds of projectiles per second will show many allocations and brief frame pauses as GC runs. A common misconception is that small objects do not matter. In aggregate they do. The practical response is to reduce allocations by reusing objects via pooling. Another strategy is to avoid generating temporary garbage in frequently called code paths. Takeaway: measure allocations, then convert high-frequency spawn/despawn objects to a pool to smooth runtime performance. A basic object pool holds a collection of pre-instantiated GameObjects and exposes methods to get and return them. The common components are a prefab reference, an initial pool size, a list or queue to store pooled instances, and two public methods: GetPooledObject and ReturnPooledObject. In Awake you instantiate the initial set of objects, call SetActive(false) on each, and add them to the list. GetPooledObject searches the list for an inactive object, activates and returns it, and optionally expands the pool if none are available. ReturnPooledObject deactivates the object via SetActive(false) and optionally resets state. Pools often use a singleton pattern for easy access, but be cautious with singletons in larger architectures. Communication with pooled objects happens via lifecycle callbacks: OnEnable is used to reset state when an object is activated, and OnDisable cancels timers or scheduled returns. Concrete example: ObjectPool. Instance. GetPooledObject returns a bullet which the player positions and activates; when the bullet collides it calls ObjectPool. Instance. ReturnPooledObject instead of Destroy. Misconception: pools eliminate the need to manage state — in reality you must explicitly reset any mutable fields. How will you ensure every pooled object begins clean?

Let's walk through a concise ObjectPool implementation. The pool holds a public prefab reference and poolSize configured in the Inspector. Awake uses a loop to Instantiate the initial objects, call SetActive(false), and add them to the pooledObjects list. GetPooledObject iterates over pooledObjects, checks activeInHierarchy, activates and returns the first inactive object. If no inactive object is found the example optionally Instantiates a new object, adds it to the list, and logs a warning that the pool expanded. ReturnPooledObject simply SetActive(false) to deactivate and return the object to the pool; you may also reset state here. A common pitfall is missing SetActive(false) when returning an object, causing the pool to incorrectly consider objects active and leak resources. The snippet provided is intentionally straightforward: it demonstrates the flow and allows you to extend it with queues, circular indices, or thread-safe patterns. Concrete example: use this pool for bullets by calling ObjectPool. Instance. GetPooledObject in your attack method and setting position and rotation before the object is used. Think about how you would add a maximum pool cap or prewarm of child components.

Pooled objects must reset mutable state when they are activated. The ProjectilePooled example shows how to use OnEnable to clear velocity, set damage, and apply a fresh force. OnEnable is called when a GameObject becomes active; this is the ideal place to reset timers, clear physics velocities, and schedule a ReturnToPool after a lifetime using Invoke. OnDisable should cancel invokes and clean up any references so the object remains safe while inactive. In collisions the projectile calls ReturnToPool instead of Destroy, ensuring it goes back to the pool and becomes available for reuse. A common mistake is to assume the constructor or Awake will reset state; Awake runs only once at load time, not each activation. Concrete example: in OnEnable set rb. velocity = Vector3. zero and then rb. AddForce(transform. forward * speed) to ensure the projectile always starts fresh. Misconception: pooling guarantees fresh behavior; in reality you must explicitly reset every variable that can carry over from previous uses. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Instantiate/Destroy is simple to implement and fine for occasional spawns such as rare pickups or one-off effects. It keeps code minimal but causes allocation overhead when used frequently. Object pooling requires more upfront work: preinstantiation, reset logic, and management of active/inactive state. The benefit is lower runtime allocation and fewer GC spikes, which translates to smoother frame rates in high-frequency scenarios. There are tradeoffs: pools consume memory for the precreated objects and may need careful sizing or dynamic expansion to avoid exhaustion. A misconception is that pools always save memory; in fact you trade memory headroom for runtime stability. Concrete scenario: for debris from a single explosion that spawns hundreds of fragments, a pool prevents repeated allocation spikes; for a rare boss drop used once each level, Instantiate/Destroy is acceptable. Key decision factors are spawn rate, object complexity, and target hardware. Final question: what is the expected spawn rate in your scene and does that justify the memory cost of a pool? Object pooling fixes allocation costs but introduces its own class of bugs if not implemented carefully. The most frequent mistakes are failing to reset an object's state, forgetting to call SetActive(false) when returning an object, and leaving Destroy calls in pooled objects. Failing to reset state might leave a projectile with previous velocity or an enemy with reduced health. Forgetting to deactivate means the pool will think the object is still active and may appear duplicated or leak behavior. Leaving Destroy in pooled code undoes the benefit of pooling by causing deallocation. Another pitfall is not planning for pool exhaustion: if your pool lacks dynamic expansion you may run out of objects at runtime. The provided pool logs a warning and creates a new instance if none are available, which is helpful during testing. Also avoid putting heavy initialization in Awake that assumes fresh instances; prefer OnEnable for runtime resets. Concrete practice: audit each pooled script and list any fields that persist across uses, then explicitly reset them on enable. Takeaway: pooling helps performance but requires deliberate, testable reset and return logic.

Testing your pool under realistic, heavy-load conditions is essential. Start by firing continuously at a high rate or spawning many particle bursts simultaneously. Observe the Hierarchy: a healthy pool will activate and deactivate existing clones under the ObjectPoolManager rather than creating and destroying new ones each frame. If your pool logs the warning about exhaustion, that indicates usage exceeded the initial poolSize and the pool dynamically instantiated a new object. Use that warning to tune poolSize or to implement an upper cap with a fallback behavior. Also watch for logical bugs: if bullets remain visible after ReturnPooledObject, you likely forgot to SetActive(false). If bullets inherit strange velocities, inspect OnEnable resets. Keep three practical ideas in mind. First, Instantiate clones a Prefab and allocates memory. Use it for occasional spawns but watch frequency. Second, Destroy marks objects for removal and participates in cleanup; this contributes to garbage-collection spikes when used often. Third, object pooling reuses pre-instantiated objects by activating and deactivating them, avoiding repeated allocation and smoothing runtime performance. Also remember to reset state in OnEnable, call SetActive(false) when returning objects, and plan for pool exhaustion. These core concepts will guide your decisions when implementing projectiles, particle effects, and any frequently spawned items.
